items.title: Transport soak scenarios are enumerated
items.statement: The plan explicitly names sleep/wake, reconnect, first-event timeout, large terminal output, high-frequency browser snapshots, and WebSocket fallback as required soak coverage.

items.title: Transport coverage is not bound to a test matrix or consumers
items.statement: The finding family names WS, SSE, terminal, browser, and device transports, but the acceptance sentence neither maps each transport to each scenario nor names the runtime callers and result consumers. items.impact: A partial implementation can claim coverage without exercising all named transport families or delivering results to their consumers.

items.title: Soak workload and pass thresholds are unbounded
items.statement: The soak requirement provides no duration, reconnect count, first-event deadline, terminal-output size, snapshot rate, concurrency, resource budget, or permitted loss/error threshold.
items.impact: Implementations can select trivial loads and incompatible pass criteria, making the requirement non-falsifiable at production scale.

items.title: Offline and network-loss fault model is incomplete

dimension_assessments.summary: Transport and cross-document consumers are named only as families or target docs, without per-scenario or per-contract bindings.
Receipt transitions and terminal-state invariants are absent, and enablement is contradicted by an unresolved deferred disposition.
Renderer lock risk is acknowledged, but stale GUI status and completion-versus-cancel races have no authoritative resolution protocol.
Receipts contain rich counters and artifacts but lack completeness, atomicity, and crashed-adapter partial-output semantics.
No disable, rollback, re-probe, or in-flight recovery transition follows loss of enablement prerequisites; cancellation cleanup is also unspecified.
Invocation, cancellation, export, and enablement omit actor authority and enforceable permission/authorization bindings.
Replay corpora and exported logs or screenshots have no governed provenance, redaction, retention, deletion, or authorization lifecycle.
Terminal streams, commands, targets, and artifacts lack validation, sandboxing, containment, and integrity limits.
Basic button derivation is explicit, but stale state, undefined terminality, unsafe export enablement, and contradictory repair status can mislead users.
Reconnect and fallback are named, but offline and partition fault models plus post-enable network-loss behavior are not specified.
Soak workloads, renderer budgets, degradation thresholds, and receipt expectations lack measurable limits.
Terminal replay compares an accessible mirror, but the test-results GUI itself lacks keyboard, focus, announcement, naming, and preview-accessibility contracts.
No locale, pluralization, formatting, translation-key, or text-overflow behavior is specified for testing results and statuses.
Fuzz corpora, invocations, receipts, adapters, and stored evidence lack a version negotiation and migration contract.
Receipt evidence references are a concrete strength, but soak execution, degradation receipts, event attribution, correlation, and consumer acknowledgement remain undefined.
Cancellation is exposed without authority, confirmation, cleanup, shared-run, repeated-action, or evidence-retention semantics.
Target documents lack explicit consumer contracts, and three repaired rows remain simultaneously marked explicitly deferred in the same core.
Concrete scenario lists exist, but soak and budget thresholds, executable commands, receipt oracles, and a coverage matrix are missing.
Without an enumerated interaction coverage manifest, it is unknown which negative-space combinations are intentional exclusions versus unseen omissions.
